correctness.rationale: The normalized product integral is Jozsa–Mitchison equation (14). Its mass-splitting difference is exactly a(w-a)t times nonnegative remaining factors over positive denominators; log-convexity of the product gives concavity of the split curve. The derivative at zero is bounded by w integral (t+w)^(-2)=1. Concavity gives 0<=delta Q<=a for every split, including endpoints by continuity. Splitting each observation probability into conditionals yields the exact total removed mass 1-pguess; a binary small-error family has derivative one and establishes sharpness. The proof includes zero probabilities and repeat spectra by continuous extension. The 48 high-precision table checks in verify_subentropy.py are corroborative, not substitutes for proof.

evidence: Jozsa–Mitchison arXiv:1404.7694 equation (14) is the half-axis integral for subentropy; its Appendix Lemma 3 and Property 9 prove monotonicity under marginalization, including the nonnegative half of the finding.
Datta et al. arXiv:1310.1312 Proposition 5 proves nonnegativity of conditional subentropy even for noncommuting signal states.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The positive lower inequality is covered and not claimed as new. Neither the general integral formula nor marginal monotonicity alone states a Bayes-error upper bound. The sharp bound requires an additional derivative comparison at the boundary of every spectral mass split, followed by telescoping over conditional observation outcomes. Generic subentropy-versus-min-entropy bounds for one state do not control a difference of two subentropies.

value.rationale: Finite commuting quantum signal ensembles form the full naturally classical sector of a named unresolved conditional-subentropy conjecture. The result settles that entire sector for arbitrary mixed signals and nonuniform priors, improves the claimed logarithmic upper bound to a dimension-independent sharp linear Bayes-error bound, and yields an explicit strictly stronger guessing-probability certificate pguess <= 1-Q. The underlying mass-splitting lemma captures the structural reason, not a finite numerical curiosity.
